cim: A new wave of U.S. layoffs raises questions about how artificial intelligence is changing job security
cim_eredeti: A new wave of U.S. layoffs raises questions about how artificial intelligence is changing job security
szoveg_eredeti:
Imagine opening your work email and learning your company is cutting jobs. Across the United States, layoff announcements are raising a question: How much of this is tied to AI?

Some employers say artificial intelligence helps them work with fewer people. Others point to costs, slower business or restructuring. The difference matters when trying to understand what workers face next.

U.S. employers cited artificial intelligence in 121,401 announced job cuts from January through October 2026, according to figures tracking company layoff plans. That represents about 20% of announced cuts nationwide.

These figures count planned reductions, not necessarily workers already unemployed. They also reflect reasons given by employers, making it difficult to determine how much work artificial intelligence actually replaced directly.

AI accounted for 1,265 announced cuts in October, its lowest monthly total of 2026. Employers increasingly pointed to market conditions instead of technology when explaining their plans for reducing staff.

Economic conditions were cited for 16,407 cuts that month. This shift does not mean AI stopped changing workplaces. It shows that the reasons behind layoffs can change as businesses respond.

The technology sector recorded 171,501 announced job cuts through October, more than any other industry in the tracking report. Its total reflects different company decisions, not just artificial intelligence adoption.

Software businesses are changing how they build products and manage employees. Some are putting more money into AI tools while trimming departments, which can leave workers uncertain about their roles.

Little-known fact: While 60% of U.S. workers fear AI will eliminate more jobs than it creates, data shows the technology is reshaping specific roles rather than causing a mass layoff wave.

Amazon announced plans in January to eliminate 16,000 corporate positions. The company described the move as an effort to reduce bureaucracy and strengthen how teams make decisions across its businesses.

The announcement followed another large corporate reduction in October 2025. Amazon has also discussed how AI may reshape staffing over time, but its January explanation centered on organizational changes instead.

Fun fact: Amazon was originally named Cadabra (short for Abracadabra), before Jeff Bezos's lawyer misheard it as "cadaver."

Home services platform Angi announced plans to eliminate approximately 300 positions on Nov. 3, 2026, mostly affecting middle management and support functions. The company said the restructuring was intended to sharpen its focus and help teams make decisions faster.

Earlier in January, Angi announced approximately 350 job reductions, citing lower operating costs, organizational changes and efficiency improvements driven by AI. The separate announcements show how a company's reasons for reducing staff can differ between restructuring rounds.

Software company Atlassian announced plans in March to cut about 1,600 jobs, roughly 10% of its workforce. The company linked the restructuring to investment priorities and changes in artificial intelligence.

Its leadership said AI changes the skills organizations need and the number of people required in certain roles. That does not mean every position eliminated was replaced by a computer.

Oracle reported that its employee count fell to about 141,000 by May 31, down roughly 21,000 from a year earlier. That decline includes workforce changes across the reporting period itself.

In its annual filing, Oracle said using AI across operations had contributed to workforce reductions and could lead to more. The statement offers a connection, without identifying every affected job.

Not every company cutting staff blames AI. Some employers cite weaker demand, costs or changes in strategy. Those reasons can overlap with technology investments without being the same thing entirely.

For example, a business may reduce management layers while expanding software spending. Calling every cut an AI replacement would overlook decisions involving sales, budgets and how teams are organized internally.

Despite major company announcements, the U.S. unemployment rate was 4.1% in October, little changed from September. Employers added 165,000 jobs that month, according to federal labor figures released in November.

Separate federal data showed 1.6 million layoffs and discharges in September, with little change from August. Individual headlines can feel alarming even when broader labor market measures remain stable overall.

An employer can eliminate one kind of job while recruiting for another. That helps explain why company layoff notices and hiring announcements can appear together, even within the same industry.

In October, employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers, according to a national tracking report. These are plans rather than completed hires, and many positions were intended for seasonal work.

A major employer survey found that 41% of participating companies expected to reduce staff as AI automates certain tasks by 2030. That forecast describes expectations, not confirmed future job losses.

The same research identified growth opportunities in technology and other fields, including care and education. Workers may benefit from learning tools while keeping the communication and judgment skills employers value.

For employees, the clearest signals often come from their workplaces. New software, changing responsibilities and revised hiring plans can offer clues about how a company expects work to change in the coming months.

National employment reports provide useful context, but they cannot predict any individual's job security. Workers can pay attention to changing skill requirements and explore opportunities to learn new tools as their industries evolve.
